sections.history: Thirukkovilur is an old town on the southern bank of the Then Pennai river in Kallakurichi district, remembered in Tamil literature as the seat of the Malaiyaman chieftains in the age of the Sangam poets. Its Shiva temple, known in older usage as Andhakapuram and Thirukkaivelur, is one of the eight Ashta Veerattanams, the shrines of the Lord's heroic deeds — here, his victory over the demon Andhaka. Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar all sang it in the Tevaram, and it is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Nadu Nadu country. Chola-period inscriptions record endowments made to the shrine. The town is a Vaishnava pilgrimage too, for the Trivikrama Perumal Divya Desam stands here; the Veerattanam is a separate temple, with its own long history.
sections.architecture: The temple stands near the river in the Dravidian manner, its gateway tower opening onto courtyards that lead to the sanctum of Veerattaneswarar, with the goddess Periyanayaki in a shrine of her own. Its treasure is its bronzes: in the first precinct are festival images of Nataraja and Somaskanda, and of Andhakasura Samhara Murthy — Shiva in the very act this Veerattanam honours, the form that is carried out in procession on festival days.
sections.legends: Andhaka, the blind demon, grew mighty through boons and turned his strength against the gods. The tale most often told of him is that every drop of his blood that touched the ground rose up as another demon, so that wounding him only multiplied the battle. Shiva pierced him with his trident and held him aloft, so that no blood could fall, until the demon's pride was spent; in many tellings Andhaka, humbled, became a devotee of the Lord. Thirukkovilur keeps this victory, and its old name Andhakapuram preserves it.
sections.festivals: The festivals of the Shaiva year are kept here — Maha Shivaratri, the fortnightly pradosham, Arudra Darshan in Margazhi and Karthigai Deepam — and the annual festival brings the bronzes, among them Andhakasura Samhara Murthy, out in procession through the streets of Thirukkovilur. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirukkovilur rewards a slower visit: a river town where a Shiva Veerattanam and a great Vishnu temple stand within the same streets, each with its own saints and songs. Pilgrims following the eight Veerattanams usually pair it with Thiruvathigai near Panruti to the east, before turning south to the Kaveri delta, where the remaining six lie.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; festival days are the busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thirukkovilur lies in Kallakurichi district on the road between Villupuram and Tiruvannamalai, roughly 35 km from each, and has a railway station on the Villupuram–Katpadi line. The nearest airports are at Puducherry and Chennai.
